question_text:
The circuit below shows a 5 V source driving an LED with a forward voltage of 2 V. The target current is 20 mA.

What resistor value limits the current to 20 mA?
answer_text:
R = 150 Ω

▶ Detailed Explanation

Apply KVL (Kirchhoff's Voltage Law) around the loop — the sum of voltage drops must equal the source:

Vcc = V_R + Vf

The resistor drops whatever is left after the LED takes its 2 V:

V_R = 5V − 2V = 3V

Ohm's Law gives the resistance:

R = V_R / I = 3V / 20 mA = 150 Ω

150 Ω is a standard E24 value — no rounding needed.
bonus_question_text: Beyond resistance value, what else should you check when specifying this resistor?
bonus_answer_text:
Two things: power rating and tolerance.

Power Rating (Wattage)

The resistor must dissipate: P = V_R × I = 3V × 20 mA = 60 mW

A 1/16 W (≈62.5 mW) resistor is right at the limit — it will run hot and can burn out. Always leave headroom: use at least 1/8 W (125 mW), giving a comfortable 2× margin.

Tolerance

A 5% tolerance 150 Ω resistor could be anywhere from 142.5 Ω to 157.5 Ω:

  • −5% → 142.5 Ω: I = 3V / 142.5 = 21.1 mA — slightly over, fine for most LEDs
  • +5% → 157.5 Ω: I = 3V / 157.5 = 19.0 mA — a hair dimmer, almost unnoticeable

Standard 5% resistors are fine in practice. Tolerance only matters if the LED's absolute maximum current rating is extremely tight — which is rare.
